units.title: Indian securities markets: an overview
units.overview: Structure of the market, its instruments and participants.
facts: Securities
Securities include shares, bonds, units of mutual funds and derivatives, as defined in the Securities Contracts (Regulation) Act.
Shares and bonds are both examples.
Securities include only shares.
Primary and secondary market
New issues take place in the primary market; trading of already issued securities occurs in the secondary market.
An IPO is a primary market event while daily trading is secondary.
The company receives money in secondary trades.
Stock exchange
A stock exchange is a recognised, regulated marketplace such as the BSE or NSE where securities trade electronically.
Buyers and sellers are matched on an online system.
An exchange decides the profits of companies.
Trading member
A trading member is a broker admitted by the exchange who can trade on the platform for clients and own account.
A SEBI-registered broker with exchange membership.
Any investor can be a trading member.
Depository
Depositories like NSDL and CDSL hold securities in electronic form through participants.
A client's shares are held through a depository participant.
A depository is a type of stock exchange.
Clearing corporation
The clearing corporation guarantees and settles trades, becoming the central counterparty.
It ensures delivery and payment for exchange trades.
The clearing corporation executes client orders.
Market segments
Exchanges offer segments for cash equity, equity derivatives, currency, commodity and debt trading.
A client may trade shares in cash and futures in derivatives.
There is only a cash segment.
Retail and institutional participants
Participants include retail investors, high-net-worth individuals, mutual funds, FPIs, banks and insurers.
Foreign portfolio investors and domestic mutual funds both trade.
Only retail investors trade on exchanges.
Dematerialisation
Dematerialisation converts paper certificates into electronic form, making trading and transfer faster and safer.
A client's shares exist in electronic form.
Dematerialisation is the process of printing shares.

units.title: Regulatory framework
units.overview: The laws and rules that apply to brokers and their clients. The most rule-heavy unit; learn exact terms.
focus: Stock broker regulations and client documentation.
visuals: Creates SEBI and sets its powers
Regulation of securities contracts and exchanges
Company law including issue of securities
facts: SEBI
SEBI protects investors, promotes market development and regulates the securities market, with powers to make regulations, investigate and penalise.
The regulator can issue circulars and levy penalties on brokers.
SEBI is a stock exchange.
SCRA 1956
The Securities Contracts (Regulation) Act governs recognition of stock exchanges and regulates the trading of securities.
The law under which exchanges are recognised.
The SCRA is the law on money laundering.
Depositories Act 1996
This law provides the legal framework for depositories and dematerialisation of securities in India.
The law behind NSDL and CDSL.
The Depositories Act governs insurance companies.
Stock broker regulations
Brokers must be registered with SEBI, be members of an exchange, meet capital adequacy and follow a code of conduct.
A broker without registration cannot deal for clients.
A broker needs no registration if it is an exchange member.
Client registration form
Each client must sign the account opening form with mandatory documents and KYC, and the broker must give a copy of the rights and obligations.
A client signs the standard form before the first trade.
Clients may trade before signing the form.
Know Your Client
KYC verifies identity and address using PAN and documents, and is mandatory for opening any trading account.
A new client provides PAN, address proof and a photograph.
KYC is optional for small investors.
Unique Client Code
The UCC is a unique code allotted to each client by the broker and mapped to the client's PAN in exchange records.
Each client's trades are tagged with a code mapped to PAN.
Clients share one code with the broker.
Contract note
A broker must issue a contract note for every trade within 24 hours of execution, showing price, time, quantity and charges.
A client gets a note after executing a trade.
A contract note is issued at the end of the year.
Power of attorney
A POA authorises the broker to perform limited acts such as pledging for margin; it must not give general trading authority and misuse is prohibited.
A client signs a limited authority for settlement-related acts.
A POA allows brokers to trade at will for the client.
Running account settlement
Brokers must settle client funds and securities at regular intervals, monthly or quarterly as chosen by the client, unless the client specifies otherwise.
A broker returns the unused client balance on schedule.
Brokers may hold client balances indefinitely.
Segregation of client funds
Client money and securities must be kept separate from the broker's own and cannot be used for proprietary trading.
A broker keeps clients' money in a separate account.
A broker may use client funds for own trades.
Insider trading regulations
SEBI's PIT regulations prohibit dealing in securities while in possession of unpublished price sensitive information.
A broker's employee trades on a leaked merger news.
Insiders may trade if they trade small amounts.
Fraudulent and unfair trade practices
The PFUTP regulations prohibit market manipulation, misleading statements and fraud in securities dealing.
Spreading false rumours to move a stock price.
PFUTP regulations apply only to issuers.
PMLA
The Prevention of Money Laundering Act requires brokers to verify customers, maintain records and report suspicious transactions to the FIU.
A broker reports an unusual cash-related pattern to the authority.
Brokers need not report suspicious transactions.
Suspicious transaction report
A broker must report suspicious transactions to the Financial Intelligence Unit when it suspects money laundering.
A broker files a report on a client with unexplained large flows.
The client must be told before a report is filed.
Investor charter
Brokers must display and share the investor charter listing investors' rights, responsibilities and grievance steps.
A client receives a document describing her rights.
The investor charter is for brokers' internal use.
Arbitration
Disputes between clients and brokers can be referred to the exchange's arbitration mechanism within the prescribed period.
A client takes an unresolved dispute to arbitration.
Clients cannot resolve disputes through exchanges.
SCORES and ODR
Clients can lodge complaints with SEBI through SCORES and use the online dispute resolution platform after approaching the broker and the exchange.
A client files a complaint on the regulator's portal.
Complaints can only be made in person.
Investor Protection Fund
Exchanges maintain a fund to compensate clients of defaulting brokers up to a limit.
A client of a defaulting broker may claim compensation from the fund.
The fund covers all trading losses.
Code of conduct
The code of conduct for brokers requires integrity, diligence, fair dealing and proper records, and prohibits unfair practices.
A broker must not promise guaranteed profits.
The code allows brokers to guarantee returns.
Margin trading facility
Brokers may offer margin funding under SEBI rules with disclosures, collecting margin and keeping the pledged securities in a separate account.
A client buys shares by funding part with the broker's money.
Margin funding needs no margin from the client.
Authorised person
Authorised persons act on behalf of brokers for acquiring clients and facilitating trades, as registered with the exchange.
An agent introduces clients to the broker.
Authorised persons may execute trades on their own.
Record retention
Brokers must maintain records of orders, trades, communications and client details for at least five years.
A broker keeps the call recording of a client order.
Records can be deleted after a month.

units.title: Primary markets
units.overview: IPOs and other issuance routes from the broker's perspective: eligibility, process, categories and allotment.
visuals: Under the standard book-building route, up to 50% goes to QIBs, at least 15% to non-institutional investors and at least 35% to retail investors, subject to SEBI's rules for each issue.
facts: SEBI ICDR Regulations
The Issue of Capital and Disclosure Requirements Regulations govern how companies raise capital, including eligibility and disclosures.
The rules that govern IPO eligibility and contents of the offer document.
The ICDR regulations govern brokerage rates.
Initial public offer
An IPO is the first sale of shares to the public by an unlisted company, followed by listing on exchanges.
A company sells shares to the public for the first time.
An IPO is a sale of shares to existing shareholders only.
Draft offer document
The draft red herring prospectus is filed with SEBI, which examines it and issues observations before the issue is launched.
A company files a draft document through a merchant banker.
SEBI approves the price in the draft document.
Book building
In book building, investors bid within a price band and the issue price is determined based on the demand.
Demand at different prices decides the final price.
The price is fixed before any bids come in.
Price band
The price band specifies the floor and cap for bids; the cap cannot exceed 120% of the floor.
Bids can be made between ₹200 and ₹240.
A price band has no cap.
Bid lot
The minimum bid lot is the smallest number of shares that can be applied for, set so that the application value is within a prescribed range.
An investor must apply for at least 50 shares.
Investors can bid for one share in any IPO.
Retail individual investor
A retail individual investor applies for shares worth up to ₹2 lakh in an issue.
An investor applies for ₹1.8 lakh worth of shares.
A retail investor can apply for ₹5 lakh in the retail category.
Non-institutional investor
NIIs apply for more than ₹2 lakh and are not QIBs, usually high-net-worth individuals and corporates.
An investor bids for ₹10 lakh of shares.
NIIs bid for less than ₹2 lakh.
Qualified institutional buyer
QIBs are institutions such as mutual funds, insurers, banks and FPIs, treated as sophisticated investors.
A mutual fund bids in the QIB category.
QIBs are retail individuals.
Anchor investor
Anchor investors are QIBs who bid a day before the issue opens for at least ₹10 crore, subject to a lock-in on their shares.
Institutions are allotted shares before the public issue opens.
Anchor investors are small retail investors.
Basis of allotment
If an issue is oversubscribed, allotment is made proportionately or by lottery in the retail category, so some applicants may get nothing.
A retail investor applies and receives no shares due to oversubscription.
Every applicant always gets the full number of shares applied.
UPI in IPO
Retail and certain other investors apply through UPI, where the money is blocked in the investor's account until allotment.
An investor approves a mandate on her UPI app.
UPI mandates debit the money immediately and never release it.
Listing timeline
Allotment and listing must be completed within three working days of the closure of the issue.
The issue closes and shares list within a few days.
Listing takes place within a month.
Promoter contribution and lock-in
Promoters must contribute at least 20% of the post-issue capital, which is locked in for 18 months.
Promoters' minimum stake is locked for a period after listing.
Promoters may sell their stake on the listing day.
Greenshoe option
A greenshoe option allows the issuer to allot extra shares up to 15% of the issue to stabilise post-listing prices.
The stabilising agent can support the price after listing.
A greenshoe option reduces the issue size.
Offer for sale
In an OFS, existing shareholders sell their shares in the issue and the company receives no proceeds.
Promoters sell part of their holding through a public offer.
The company receives proceeds from an OFS.
Rights issue
A rights issue offers existing shareholders the right to subscribe to new shares in proportion to their holding.
A company offers one new share for each four held.
A rights issue is offered to new investors only.
QIP
A Qualified Institutions Placement lets a listed company issue shares only to QIBs without a full public offering.
A listed company sells shares to institutions at a price near the market.
A QIP is available to retail investors.
Preferential issue
A preferential issue allots shares to a selected group at a price determined as per SEBI's pricing rules.
A company issues shares to a strategic investor.
A preferential issue is offered to all shareholders equally.
Buyback
A buyback is the repurchase by a company of its own shares, reducing outstanding shares, via tender offer or open market.
A company repurchases shares at a premium.
A buyback increases the number of shares.
SME IPO
SME exchanges allow smaller companies to raise money with lighter norms but with larger lots and more risk.
A small firm lists on a dedicated platform.
SME IPOs follow the same rules as main-board IPOs.
Merchant banker
A merchant banker manages the issue process, due diligence and regulatory filings, and is registered with SEBI.
The lead manager of an IPO.
A merchant banker is the registrar who allots shares.
Underwriting
An underwriter commits to subscribe to the unsubscribed portion of an issue, giving certainty to the issuer.
A firm promises to take up shares not subscribed by the public.
An underwriter guarantees a profit to investors.

units.title: Secondary markets
units.overview: How the exchange market works for cash equity.
facts: Trading session
Regular equity trading takes place from 9:15 am to 3:30 pm, preceded by a pre-open session from 9:00 am to 9:15 am.
An investor places an order at 11 am on a working day.
Equity trading runs all night.
Pre-open session
The pre-open session uses a call auction between 9:00 and 9:15 am to determine opening prices.
An order is placed before the market opens to discover the opening price.
The pre-open session executes trades continuously.
Order matching
Orders are matched by price-time priority: best price first and, at the same price, earliest order first.
An earlier bid at the same price is filled first.
Orders are matched by size alone.
Tick size
The tick size is the minimum price movement, generally ₹0.05 for equity shares.
A price can change in steps of five paise.
Tick size is the number of shares in a lot.
Market lot
In the equity cash segment the market lot is one share, so investors can trade any quantity.
An investor buys 7 shares of a company.
The cash segment requires a lot of 100 shares.
Trading segments
Segments include normal, trade-for-trade and surveillance-restricted ones, each with different conditions on trading.
A stock in a restricted segment cannot be squared off intraday.
All stocks trade under the same conditions.
Types of trades
Trades are classified as delivery-based or intraday (squared off within the day), with different charges and margins.
A client buys and sells within the day without taking delivery.
Intraday trades require delivery at the end of the day.

units.title: Market indicators
units.overview: Indices and signals used to read the market.
facts: Sensex
The Sensex is the BSE's 30-stock benchmark, weighted by free-float market capitalisation.
An index of 30 companies on the Bombay exchange.
The Sensex has 50 stocks.
Nifty 50
The Nifty 50 represents 50 large companies on the NSE, weighted by free-float market capitalisation.
An index of 50 leading companies on the National exchange.
The Nifty 50 has 30 stocks.
Free-float method
The free-float method counts only publicly available shares, excluding promoter holdings, to weight stocks in an index.
A stock with high promoter holding gets less weight.
The free-float method counts all shares.
Sectoral and broad indices
Sectoral indices track specific industries like banks, while broad indices such as the Nifty 500 represent the wider market.
An index tracking only banks is sectoral.
Sectoral indices cover the whole market.
Market breadth
Breadth compares the number of advancing and declining stocks, showing how widespread a market move is.
The index rises but declining stocks outnumber advancing ones.
Breadth shows the daily turnover.
India VIX
India VIX measures the market's expectation of near-term volatility, derived from index option prices.
A rising reading indicates greater expected volatility.
India VIX measures interest rates.
Market turnover
Turnover is the total value of securities traded in a period, showing market activity and liquidity.
The day's total traded value in the cash market.
Turnover is the total market capitalisation.
FPI and DII flows
Net buying or selling by FPIs and DIIs is tracked daily as it influences market direction.
Foreign investors sell heavily and the index falls.
Institutional flows have no effect on prices.
Market P/E
The index P/E divides the index's total market value by total earnings and shows whether the market is richly valued.
The Nifty trades at 22 times earnings.
Index P/E shows the number of stocks.
52-week high and low
The 52-week high and low are the highest and lowest prices in the past year, used as reference for momentum and risk.
A stock hits a new yearly high.
52-week high is the highest price ever.
Put-call ratio
The put-call ratio compares put and call volumes or open interest and is a sentiment indicator.
A high ratio suggests defensive positioning.
The put-call ratio measures dividends.
Impact cost
Impact cost is the cost of executing a standard-size order beyond the ideal price and measures liquidity.
A large order moves the price against the buyer.
Impact cost is the brokerage charged.
Beta of stock
Beta shows how sensitive a stock is to market movements; above 1 is more volatile than the index.
A stock moves 1.5 times the market.
A beta of 1 means the stock is risk free.

units.title: Trading and risk management
units.overview: The largest unit: orders, margins and how brokers control risk. The details of margins and surveillance frequently appear.
visuals: Daily limits on individual stock movement
facts: Market order
A market order executes at once at the best available price and offers no control over the price.
A client wants to buy right away.
A market order specifies the price in advance.
Limit order
A limit order is executed only at the specified price or better.
A buyer states a maximum price of ₹100.
A limit order is always executed.
Stop-loss order
A stop-loss order is triggered when price hits a specified level and is meant to limit losses.
An order to sell if the price falls to ₹90.
A stop-loss order ensures a profit.
Immediate or cancel
An IOC order is executed immediately in full or part, and any unfilled portion is cancelled.
An order fills partly at once and the rest is cancelled.
An IOC order stays open all day.
Order validity
Orders can be day orders, valid until the end of the trading day, or have other validity depending on the platform.
An order lapses if not executed by the close.
All orders remain active for a year.
After-market order
An AMO is placed after market hours to be processed at the next day's open.
A client places an order at night for the next morning.
An AMO is executed immediately at night.
Price band
A price band is the maximum percentage a stock can move in a day; orders outside the band are rejected.
A stock with a 5% band cannot rise 8% in a day.
A price band is the minimum trade size.
Index circuit breaker
Market-wide circuit breakers pause trading when the benchmark index falls or rises by 10%, 15% or 20%.
Trading halts when the index drops 10%.
Circuit breakers apply to a single client.
VaR margin
VaR margin is collected to cover the potential loss in a stock over a short period at a given confidence level.
A margin that estimates the likely one-day loss.
VaR margin is a brokerage charge.
Extreme loss margin
ELM is an additional margin to cover losses beyond those estimated by VaR in extreme moves.
A buffer on top of the main margin.
ELM replaces VaR margin.
Mark-to-market margin
MTM margin covers notional losses on open positions based on current prices and is collected from the client.
A client whose position has fallen pays extra margin.
MTM margin is collected only on profit.
Peak margin
Peak margin requires the client to maintain margin for the highest intraday exposure, not just end-of-day.
A client must hold margin for the biggest position taken in the day.
Margin is calculated only at the close.
Exposure limit
Brokers set exposure limits for each client based on margin and risk, to control the risk of default.
A client cannot take positions beyond her limit.
Exposure limits are the same for all clients.
Margin shortfall penalty
A shortfall in required margin attracts penalties from the exchange, which the broker may pass on to the client.
A client fails to maintain margin and is charged.
There is no penalty for a margin shortfall.
Trade-for-trade segment
In the trade-for-trade segment, each trade must be settled by delivery, and intraday squaring off is not allowed.
A stock under restriction must be taken in delivery.
In T2T, positions can be netted off in the day.
Additional surveillance measure
ASM places stocks under additional margins and restrictions when there is a surge in price or volume that is unusual.
An exchange flags a stock after an abnormal rise.
ASM is a measure to reward high volume.
Short selling
Short selling means selling shares one does not own, with the obligation to deliver later; naked short selling is not allowed for delivery settlement.
An investor sells today expecting to buy back cheaper.
Short selling profits when prices rise.
BTST
Buy Today Sell Tomorrow lets a client sell shares the next day before they are received in demat, with associated risks of auction.
A client buys today and sells tomorrow before delivery.
BTST means the client must hold the shares for a month.
Intraday trading
Intraday trades are squared off within the same day, so no delivery is taken, and profits or losses are settled in cash.
A client buys and sells within the day.
Intraday trades always lead to delivery.
Collateral and pledge
Clients pledge securities to the broker as margin through the depository, with the securities remaining in the client's demat account.
A client pledges shares to get margin credit.
Pledged shares are transferred to the broker's name.
Client-level risk monitoring
Brokers monitor client positions in real time and may square off positions when margin falls below required levels.
A broker closes a client's position when margin runs out.
A broker cannot act without the client's call.
Error trade handling
Erroneous trades should be identified and handled as per exchange rules, with documentation and client communication.
A trade placed at a wrong price is reviewed and corrected.
Brokers may ignore errors that favour them.
Price discovery
Price discovery is the process by which buy and sell orders interact to set the market price.
The price changes as buyers and sellers place orders.
The exchange sets prices by decree.
Auction
If a seller fails to deliver shares, an auction is conducted to buy the shares for the buyer, and the seller bears the loss.
A short delivery leads to an auction.
An auction happens when the buyer fails to pay.
Circular trading and risk
Brokers must monitor trading patterns for circular trades and other manipulative activity and report to the exchange.
A broker flags matched trades between related accounts.
Circular trading need not be reported.

units.title: Clearing and settlement
units.overview: How a trade turns into delivery and payment.
facts: Rolling settlement
In rolling settlement, trades done each day are settled after a fixed number of days, now T+1 for equity.
A trade on Monday is settled on Tuesday.
Equity settlement takes place weekly.
Pay-in and pay-out
Pay-in is the delivery of securities and funds to the clearing corporation, and pay-out is the release to the buyer and seller.
Sellers deliver shares and buyers pay money, and then each receives what is due.
Pay-out is the payment to the clearing corporation.
Clearing member
A clearing member settles trades with the clearing corporation for itself or others.
An entity that deals with the clearing corporation for trades.
A clearing member advises clients on shares.
Novation
Novation substitutes the clearing corporation as counterparty to each trade, guaranteeing settlement.
After the trade, the buyer and seller each deal with the clearing corporation.
Novation ends the trade.
Settlement guarantee fund
The settlement guarantee fund is a pool maintained by the clearing corporation to complete settlement when a member defaults.
A fund exists to complete settlements if a broker fails.
The fund pays profits to clients.
Delivery instruction
A client instructs the depository participant to transfer shares for settlement using a delivery instruction slip or electronic authorisation.
A seller authorises transfer of shares to settle her sale.
Delivery instructions are used to place orders.
Short delivery
If the seller fails to deliver, the shortage is settled through an auction or closed out at a set price.
The seller does not deliver, and the exchange auctions the shares.
A short delivery is cancelled with no consequences.
Close-out
Close-out is the compulsory settlement of a position that cannot be delivered, at a price determined by the exchange.
A seller who cannot deliver sees the trade closed out at a specified price.
Close-out is the buyer's penalty.
Funds settlement
Funds are settled through clearing banks, with the clearing corporation debiting and crediting member accounts.
The exchange moves funds between members' bank accounts.
Funds are settled only in cash at the broker's office.
Settlement calendar
The exchange publishes a settlement calendar, including holidays, to determine pay-in and pay-out dates.
A trade near a holiday settles after the holiday.
Settlement dates are the same irrespective of holidays.
Corporate action adjustments
Settlement of trades around corporate actions follows the ex-date, with the buyer entitled only if bought before the ex-date.
A buyer on the ex-date does not get the dividend.
A buyer on the ex-date is entitled to the dividend.
Settlement default
If a member defaults, the clearing corporation uses the member's deposits and other resources to complete obligations.
The member's margin is used to settle.
The clients of the defaulting member always lose everything.

units.title: Market surveillance
units.overview: How exchanges and brokers detect and deter market abuse.
facts: Market manipulation
Market manipulation is any activity that artificially moves prices or volumes, such as rigging or spreading false news.
A group trades among themselves to inflate a stock's volume.
Market manipulation is legal if the trades are small.
Pump and dump
In a pump and dump, promoters inflate a stock's price with hype, then sell to the public at the high.
A stock is promoted by misleading messages before insiders sell.
A pump and dump is a legitimate strategy.
Front running
Front running is trading ahead of a client's large order to profit from the expected price impact.
A dealer buys for himself before executing a client's big buy order.
Front running is permitted if the client is not harmed.
Surveillance alerts
Exchanges and brokers generate alerts on unusual price, volume, client concentration or order patterns.
A system flags a sudden surge in a stock's volume.
Surveillance covers only derivatives.
Graded surveillance measure
GSM places stocks with a mismatch between price and fundamentals in graded stages with restrictions on trading.
A stock whose price is far above earnings is placed in a restricted stage.
GSM is a reward for strong stocks.
Reporting obligations
Brokers must report suspicious trades and clients to the exchange and regulators and keep records of alerts and actions.
A broker flags a series of suspicious trades to the exchange.
Brokers need not report anything about client trades.
Penalties for abuse
SEBI can impose monetary penalties, bar participants from the market and prosecute those involved in abuse.
A manipulator is barred and fined.
Market abuse carries no penalty.
Know your client and surveillance
KYC details help the broker spot clients whose trading pattern does not match their declared profile.
A student with a small income suddenly trades large amounts.
KYC has no role in surveillance.

units.title: Client management
units.overview: Dealing with clients correctly: onboarding, communication, suitability and complaints.
facts: Client onboarding
Onboarding includes KYC, risk profiling, signing documents and explaining services, fees and risks.
A new client completes forms and receives a welcome kit.
Onboarding is complete when the first order is placed.
Risk profiling
Understanding the client's income, experience and tolerance helps in providing suitable products and avoiding mis-selling.
A dealer asks about a client's experience before enabling derivatives.
Risk profiling is optional.
Suitability
A dealer should recommend only products and trades suitable to the client's profile and avoid pushing high-risk trades to inexperienced clients.
A dealer advises a first-time investor on the risks of leverage.
A dealer should encourage maximum trading to earn brokerage.
Disclosures
Brokers must disclose brokerage, charges, risks, and the grievance process clearly to clients.
A dealer tells the client the full list of charges.
Brokers may hide charges.
Unauthorised trading
Trading in a client's account without her instructions is prohibited and exposes the broker to penalties.
A dealer places trades without asking the client.
Dealers may trade freely in an account with consent given once for all.
Churning
Churning is excessive trading in a client's account to generate brokerage rather than serving the client's needs.
A dealer pushes a client to trade repeatedly for commission.
Churning benefits the client.
Confidentiality
Client information must be kept confidential and shared only with consent or as legally required.
A dealer does not share a client's holdings with others.
A dealer may share client data freely.
Complaint handling
Complaints must be recorded, acknowledged and resolved within prescribed timelines, with escalation to the exchange or SEBI if unresolved.
A firm logs a complaint and responds within the time limit.
Complaints can be ignored if the client is wrong.
Dormant accounts
Accounts with no activity for a defined period are marked dormant and need re-verification before use.
A client who has not traded for years must update KYC.
Dormant accounts are closed automatically.
Honest communication
Staff must not make false statements, promise returns or give tips as guaranteed outcomes.
A dealer says there is no risk in a trade.
A dealer may assure profits to build trust.
Conflict of interest
Staff must avoid conflicts, such as trading ahead of clients, and disclose any that cannot be avoided.
A dealer discloses that he holds the stock he recommends.
Conflicts are not relevant in broking.
Record keeping and statements
Brokers must provide periodic statements of accounts and holdings and maintain records for the specified period.
A client receives monthly statements of funds and securities.
Brokers need not give statements.
